CausalChain: Chronic liver inflammation and fibrosis -> Hepatocyte transformation and genomic instability -> Altered exosome biogenesis -> Enhanced secretion of specific microRNAs targeting the HGF/MET and angiogenic pathways -> Promotion of tumor vascular invasion and immune evasion -> Changes in serum biomarker profiles (e.g., AFP variants, DCP) -> Differential therapeutic response to immunotherapy and anti-angiogenic treatments
Hypothesis: Exosome-derived microRNA profiles, particularly those modulating the HGF/MET and angiogenesis pathways, serve as sensitive early diagnostic biomarkers for HCC and can predict patient-specific responses to immunotherapy and anti-angiogenic treatment, thereby enabling more personalized therapeutic strategies.
Abstract: Recent advances in the understanding of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) have underscored the challenges of early diagnosis and tailoring treatment strategies based on conventional serum biomarkers such as AFP, AFP-L3, and DCP. Building on insights regarding the heterogeneity of HCC, the regulatory role of oncogenic pathways (including the HGF/MET axis), and the emerging utility of liquid biopsy techniques, we propose a novel hypothesis centered on exosome-derived microRNAs. These small non-coding RNAs, secreted by transformed hepatocytes in the context of chronic liver inflammation, may regulate key processes such as angiogenesis, immune evasion, and tumor vascular invasion. Their specific expression profiles could serve as early, sensitive indicators of HCC development, while also stratifying patients based on predicted responses to immunotherapy and anti-angiogenic treatments. This concept not only offers a promising avenue for better elucidating HCC pathogenesis but also for integrating biomarker discovery with personalized therapeutic approaches.
